title: A hymn in Suhi
hookLine: Suhi holds the Lavan, and Guru Nanak's paired poems of the unskilled and the skilled bride

lines: CAN SHE COOK, CAN HE EARN.
cards: Skills. Job applications ask for them, dating profiles hint at them, and family weddings have their own unwritten list: can she cook, can he earn, will they fit in.
In the Suhi section of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak sets two poems side by side. One is called Kuchaji, the unskilled bride. The next is Suchaji, the skilled bride.
And the skill that wins the second poem its name is on nobody's list. Today: a hymn in Suhi.

teach.b: First, the setting. Suhi holds the Lavan, the four rounds that marry a Sikh couple; you walked them earlier on this path. Near them sit poems where the bride is the soul and the husband is the Lord.

teach.h: KUCHAJI: I'M UNSKILLED, FULL OF FAULTS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: I'm unskilled, with faults beyond counting; how can I go to my Husband? The other brides seem each one better than the next; who would even know my name?
The friends who have enjoyed their Lord sit in the shade of the mango trees. I have none of their virtues. It's a list of failures, said out loud, without dressing it up.
Third, the skilled bride, and the surprise. She doesn't list talents.
In paraphrase: when you are with me, I have everyone; you, my Master, are all my wealth. With you within, I live in peace.

teach.h: THRONE OR BEGGING BOWL, BY YOUR WILL.
teach.b: Then the line that turns the poem: by your will come thrones and greatness, and by your will a beggar's wandering. She isn't skilled because life went well.
She can say the same thing on a throne and with a begging bowl: whatever comes, you are my wealth. Fourth, together. The poems hand out no prizes for beauty, wit or cooking.
The unskilled bride's honesty about her faults is where the path begins. The skilled bride's skill is acceptance of the Lord's will, which Sikhs call bhana.

how: Guru Nanak's Kuchaji and Suchaji are sung in kirtan in Raga Suhi, and some Sikh teachers use them to explain bhana, acceptance of God's will; the Lavan in the same raga are sung at the Anand Karaj.

games.q: what does “a hymn in suhi” mean?
o: Guru Nanak's poems of two brides, one skilled in accepting
a wedding hymn listing a good wife's household skills
a song the bride's friends sing in the mango shade

games.q: two brides in Suhi — tap the pairs.

s: the skilled bride is skilled at cooking and keeping house
her skill is saying you are my wealth, whether the Lord's will brings a throne or a beggar's wandering.
the unskilled bride hides her faults
she names them out loud, without excuses.
the bride in these poems stands for the soul
the bride is the soul and the husband is the Lord.

games.q: you're the bride in Suchaji. one season brings a throne; the next, a begging bowl. what do you say?
o: thank God for the throne and complain about the bowl.
both come by your will; you are my wealth.
games.why: by your will thrones and greatness, by your will a beggar's wandering. her skill is that you are my wealth holds in both.

practice: Let one fault come to mind, plainly, the way the unskilled bride names hers, without a speech of excuses.

Then set beside it one thing in your life that's going well and one that isn't, and hold them both in open hands, the throne and the bowl, with one Waheguru over both if you pray, or simply side by side if you don't.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Suhi. Guru Nanak's paired poems: Kuchaji, the bride who names her faults, and Suchaji, whose skill is to say you are my wealth on a throne or with a bowl. Today's word.

orig.note: suchaji, the skilled bride; kuchaji is her unskilled sister poem.

carryVoice: Your line: the skilled bride. On a throne or with a bowl: you are my wealth. See you tomorrow.
